summary: Observation of a disc-shaped luminous phenomenon.
description: Recent testimony (February 19, 2010) of an earlier sighting: on December 26 or 27, 2000, between 9:00 and 10:30 PM, several members of the same family observed a very bright disc in the sky and experienced power outages and interference on their television. No unusual noises were heard during the observation of the object, which moved and disappeared instantly. This old case, without a precise date or time and without a police report from the time, makes any investigation impossible due to a lack of information.

summary: Preservation of an ultralight aircraft intended for cinema
description: On November 11, 2000, a witness observed a disc-shaped craft with three legs. This craft flew rapidly at low altitude without making any noise. A similar observation was made by a police officer who reported hearing an engine noise. The investigation conducted by the police revealed that it was a test of a prototype ultralight aircraft intended for filming birds and for use in the film "Winged Migration".

summary: Observation of a meteorite by two crews of two airliners.
description: On November 3 at 19:25 UTC, the crews of two airliners bound for and departing from Paris observed a luminous green phenomenon with a fire-colored trail on a downward trajectory corresponding to the passage of a meteorite.

summary: A large grey ball passed a few meters above the cockpit of an airliner.
description: On October 8, 2000, at 5:04 PM UTC, the pilot and co-pilot of a flight bound for Grenoble, during its climb phase, observed a round object passing very quickly (a few tenths of a second) a few meters above the cockpit. The crew feared a collision between the object and the tail. No balloon could be identified. The possibility of a large bird (goose) was also considered, but the investigation failed to identify this sighting, which jeopardized the safety of the flight.

summary: Probable observation of a celestial body
description: On September 21, 2000, a witness returning home from work around 5:00 AM observed a luminous object with a series of colors through binoculars for approximately two hours. The object moved rapidly and erratically without making any noise. It disappeared with sunrise. No further information was gathered about this observation, which was likely that of a celestial body.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On September 10, 2000, at approximately 10:50 AM, two separate witnesses observed the simultaneous fall of two incandescent, luminous spheres with a significant white trail. No sound was detected, and the objects disappeared within seconds. This was likely an observation of atmospheric reentry.

summary: Fleeting observation of the silent movement of a triangular shape with lights: lack of reliable information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D, is part of a set of cases recently re-examined. On September 1, 2000, at approximately 5:30 AM (around 3:30 AM UTC), a man briefly glimpsed a geometric shape of luminous points in the form of a triangle. The UFO disappeared behind a building. No noise was heard. No other witness statements were collected. The routine investigation conducted by the then-GEIPAN (SEPRA) with air traffic control showed that the airport radar confirmed the recording of three unidentified traffic trails detected at 5:40 AM southeast of Toulouse. The recording, which was not confirmed by the military authorities, was entrusted to the radar specialists of the DGAC (French Civil Aviation Authority) for analysis. The result of the analysis was conclusive: these trails were not significant. They actually originated from spurious feedback caused by an aircraft flying beyond the radar's effective range. The coincidence with the witness's observation initially led to the belief that the observation was confirmed. This was not the case. GEIPAN then classified the observation itself as unexplained. A review of this case 18 years later found nothing to add to the analysis of the radar artifact. However, the unexplained nature of the observation can no longer be considered valid given the consistency of the testimony. This testimony is very imprecise: - what was orange, the bright points or the entire shape? Based on the witness's drawing, one might think it was only the bright points, but then what does the witness mean by "shape"? In the GEIPAN experiment, many witnesses believe they see a solid shape connecting bright points (and isolated ones) in the sky; - how long did the observation last? The expression "I barely had time to glimpse it" could mean a fraction of a second or 10 seconds. In the first case, one could consider shooting stars or even a meteoroid reentry with fragmentation, but this would require knowing the angular spacing of the points (size of the triangle), and whether or not there were halos. In the second case (observation lasting 10 seconds), the first hypothesis (shooting stars or atmospheric reentry) is ruled out. Based on the shape of the points of light and the behavior of the light, one could consider a flock of white birds backlit by city lights (a misinterpretation already recorded; search for cases on www.geipan.fr using the keyword "bird"). We only know that the light moved from north to southwest, which contradicts the idea of objects carried by the wind, which originates from the south (7 km/h). There are too many unanswered questions to explore, confirm, or refute the hypotheses that GEIPAN has learned to formulate (perhaps not the case 18 years ago) when a witness sees several points of light in a triangle. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Observation of the evolution of a circular shape in the sky followed by a red dot moving on the hood of a car: very likely observation of skytracers or lasers.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named LILLE (59) 2000, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On Sunday, August 20, 2000, starting at 11:30 PM, a motorist observed a moving object in the sky, shaped like a large circle made up of luminous "windows." The witness followed this object for approximately 8 km before it disappeared. Further on, when he stopped, the witness observed a red dot on his hood, moving erratically. Looking up, he again saw the same stationary circular phenomenon above his car. After a few seconds, the phenomenon disappeared, along with the red dot. Only one witness statement was recorded. The description may have seemed strange during the initial analysis of the case in 2000. With the experience acquired by GEIPAN, there is little doubt today. The description is consistent with reflections in the sky from a set of spotlights (also commonly called skytrackers) used for advertising purposes (see the investigation report). The upward beams from the spotlights are not visible here, only the impacts on a screen of sky. The pattern formed by these impacts is typical of the scanning and rotation capabilities of the devices used in nightclubs at that time, as evidenced by other observations reported to GEIPAN, where the investigation led to the recovery of the equipment producing such effects (see the case of ILE BOUCHARD (37) 11.12.1993 /index.php?id=202&cas=1993-12-01340">ILE BOUCHARD). In the GEIPAN experiment, various configurations can be encountered: visibility of the impacts alone, of the beams alone, or of both simultaneously. This depends on the weather conditions. Here, the presence of clouds that could create a screen in the sky, as well as recent rain that could have cleared the atmosphere of any water droplets that might make the rising beams visible, is being verified (it is the presence of particles in the air that allows for this visibility). It was a weekend evening in summer, in a resort area (the Normandy coast: Deauville, Trouville). This was conducive to the opening of nightclubs and other establishments using such spotlights (discos, etc.), as we know they were already widely used at the time. Regarding the second UFO, it strongly resembles the effect of a portable red laser operated by a prankster from nearby houses or buildings: this is plausible, although unverifiable. It's understandable that the witness, already experiencing the strangeness of the first phenomenon, might have associated it with the second. Without the first UFO and the resulting alertness, he might not have noticed the second or been intrigued enough to report it. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case according to the first UFO. The evidence is weak, lacking, in particular, data on angular dimensions and positions in the sky. Nevertheless, the conformity of the appearance in the sky and the weather conditions allows us to conclude with confidence (although the original projector could not be identified): observation of skytracers or lasers is very likely.

summary: Observation of a point of light: lack of information.
description: On August 15, 2000, at approximately 10:30 PM, a witness observed a very bright point of light, larger than a star. This point moved very slowly and then suddenly accelerated before disappearing within two seconds. No further information is available.

summary: Observation of the passage of points of light.
description: Recent report (October 23, 2009) of an earlier observation. Three people observed, during the summer of 2008 (though the year remains uncertain), around 11 PM, several luminous points silently passing in single file across the sky at high altitude. These points, varying in brightness, crossed the sky very quickly, likely in a south-south direction, with a slightly elliptical trajectory. The phenomenon faded below the horizon. No other reports concerning this phenomenon have been collected. In the absence of precise information, particularly regarding the date, and given the age of the observation, any investigation is difficult, if not impossible.

summary: Observation of the SE passage of a green luminous phenomenon: probable atmospheric reentry.
description: On August 1, 2000, at 1:20 a.m., two people in an apartment observed a green, ovoid-shaped object in the sky moving southeast at very high speed along a straight trajectory. The observation lasted six seconds before the object split in two and disappeared into the urban landscape. No other reports of this phenomenon have been collected. Based on the information provided, these individuals likely observed an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry
description: On July 31, 2000, at approximately 1:30 a.m., several witnesses observed a luminous sphere passing by for a few seconds before it gradually faded. The observed phenomenon was likely an atmospheric reentry, either natural or artificial.

summary: Observations of animated circles in the sky: observations of disco projector animation.
description: On July 29, 2000, at approximately 12:30 a.m., several members of the same family observed large, luminous circles in the sky, spinning like a top. The investigation revealed that this was the light effect of a disco light show reflecting off a cloud.

summary: Observations of unusual movements of flashing white lights in the sky: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named SAINT-AFFRIQUE (12) 2000, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On July 21, 2000, at approximately 11:30 PM, a man and his son were observing the sky. They suddenly noticed, with the naked eye, five flashing white lights. The trajectories of these lights were short; some turned around before disappearing. The observation lasted 5 minutes. The lights disappeared one after another. The sighting of flashing white lights moving in a linear fashion across the sky is indicative of an airplane. What alerted the witnesses was the trajectories with U-turns and the sudden appearance and disappearance of these lights. Nevertheless, the airplane hypothesis, even if it could not be a commercial airliner, remains possible and the most probable (military or general aviation aircraft), in conjunction with the presence of some clouds that could have obscured the planes. The data that would have allowed confirmation or refutation of this hypothesis was not (or could not be) collected at the time of the witness statement and is not available today. (We only have data from Météociel) from Millau, 30 km away, indicating a not completely clear sky at 4 PM. This hypothesis has the advantage of fully explaining the observation while remaining within the realm of possibility or probability. The lack of corroboration prevents us from accepting this as an explanation for the observation, but this same possibility also precludes (in light of GEIPAN's current methodology, see GEIPAN news) considering this observation as strange and unexplained. We consider this observation to be only slightly strange and lacking sufficient information to support the otherwise plausible aircraft hypothesis. GEIPAN classifies this case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Probable observation of aerial maneuvers
description: On June 27, 2000, around 11:00 PM, several witnesses observed objects with lights of different colors flying over houses. Their trajectories varied depending on the observation point. Although the witnesses described them as flying saucer-like, it is likely that these sightings were of Mirage 2000 fighter jets, which were conducting maneuvers in the area until 2:00 AM.

summary: Observation of a dark object passing by at high speed
description: On May 14, 2000, at 8:53 PM, a witness observed a dark object moving at high speed. No sound was detected. The witness estimated the object's altitude at 300 meters and its observation distance at 500 meters. No other information was collected.

summary: Observation of two luminous orbs passing 10 minutes apart
description: On March 4, 2000, at approximately 11:15 PM, a couple living near their home twice observed, 10 minutes apart, a round, yellowish-white object moving at an altitude of 15 to 20 meters. At the end of its trajectory, a faint noise was heard, accompanied by a green light. No other sounds were detected. The observed phenomenon could be interpreted as a rotating lighthouse, but the available information does not allow for a thorough analysis.

summary: Observation of the passage of an object surrounded by yellow flames: probable observation of a bolide.
description: This sighting case was classified as Category D in 2000 by SEPRA. It was re-examined (see the Investigation Notes document). On February 11, 2000, at 3:45 a.m., a motorist on his way to work suddenly observed, approximately 30 meters above the ground, an elongated object shaped like an aircraft engine, surrounded by what appeared to be yellow flames and followed by a very large, non-dazzling yellow trail. The object moved slowly along a horizontal trajectory, without making any noise. The witness stopped and got out of his car, but the phenomenon had already disappeared: in fact, the witness only glimpsed it long enough to see it pass in front of his vehicle. During the investigation, no air traffic was identified, nor were any disturbances detected on nearby power lines. This case is consistent, and the description of the observed UFO is quite precise. The witness's sincerity and credibility have never been questioned. It is not the witness's visual perception that is at issue, but rather the witness's interpretation of their observation based on their feelings (night driving, astonishment, surprise at not seeing an aircraft shape). The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color, movement, etc.) with a known astronomical phenomenon: a fireball. In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as UAP B, a probable observation linked to a natural fireball.

summary: Observation of a slowly moving luminous sphere
description: In the early hours of February 5, 2000, at approximately 2:00 AM, a witness driving a car observed a luminous phenomenon moving slowly and then coming to a stop above a wooded area. The phenomenon was silent and, according to the witness, was located about 200 meters away and 150 meters above the ground. The observation lasted approximately 30 to 40 seconds. No further information was available.

summary: Observations a few days apart by two motorists of a bright light and malfunctioning vehicles: lack of reliable information.
description: GEIPAN conducts re-examinations of old cases in order to be more relevant in its conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the past few years, this re-examination sometimes leads to a change in classification. The present re-examination concerns two observation cases previously classified as D and named BROYES (51) 10.01.2000 and SOMMESOUS (51) 31.12.1999. On January 10, 2000, between 9:00 PM and 9:05 PM, a motorist on the D39 near the Broyes (51) water tower was suddenly blinded by a very intense light that entered the car through the sunroof. The engine and the car radio stopped abruptly, but the ignition remained on. According to the witness, after a minute, the phenomenon dissipated, the car radio started working again, and he was able to restart his car and drive home, terrified. Following a phone call from the Gendarmerie's Operations Center, officers immediately went to the home of the deeply shaken witness and then to the location of the sighting. They observed that the sky was clear and full of stars (shooting stars) and that air traffic was significant and visible (flashing lights). The temperature was wintry but without frost. No disruption to the power lines along the road was observed. Furthermore, there was no street lighting in that area. According to military sources, no flights were reported that evening. The on-site investigation by SEPRA and the reconstruction in the vehicle determined that the sighting lasted between 15 and 30 seconds maximum, instead of the one minute initially reported by the witness. During the investigation, the gendarmerie found another witness who had observed a similar phenomenon a few days earlier. On December 31, 1999, between 7:30 and 8:00 PM, a motorist driving on the N4 near Sommesous (51) was blinded by a white flash. No sound was heard. All the dashboard lights came on, and the car's engine suddenly stopped, putting the car in neutral. The engine quickly restarted on its own. A check by a mechanic, initiated by the witness, of the battery terminals revealed nothing abnormal. We have two cases of observation with close spatial (a few kilometers) and temporal (10 days) proximity, presenting a strong apparent similarity (see the single investigation report for both cases): - an unlocalized light (or flash) perceived by the driver of a car; - Engine stopped, dashboard malfunctions. The case of BROYES (51) 10.01.2000 is even stranger insofar as the light was blinding and entered the vehicle. No physical explanation can be considered, the description is so bizarre. We can only formulate the hypothesis of strangeness induced or accentuated by the witness himself, but we have no evidence to support this: - the witness watched the X-Files series on television shortly before the events, when M6 was broadcasting season 4, which contains a scene where a UFO flies over a vehicle and illuminates it with a dazzling white light. The witness may have experienced a genuine strangeness that evening and been influenced, consciously or unconsciously, by science fiction when remembering or recounting the events; - The young witness, living with his parents, may have been traumatized by an event unrelated to the UFO and unable, for a reason related to his occasional drug use (self-reported) or for some other reason, to explain his condition to his parents upon returning home other than by inventing an experience directly inspired by The X-Files. In the case of SOMMESOUS (51) on December 31, 1999, the physical hypotheses (meteor, camera flash, or firework burst a few hours before the turn of the millennium) lack any supporting evidence. The consistency of these observation cases is POOR. Case of Broyes (51) 10/01/2000: - In terms of information, although an investigation was conducted on site by the gendarmerie and SEPRA (GEIPAN at the time) shortly after the events, we only have a brief report of this investigation. No audio, video, or written recordings of the various interviews and reconstructions that took place during this investigation are included in the file; - In terms of reliability, one can question the possible influence of science fiction given the similarity of the account to a scene from the X-Files series (see above). One can also question the influence of occasional drug use (see above). In the case of SOMMESOUS (51) on December 31, 1999: - in terms of information: the gendarmerie conducted no investigation beyond the witness's interview because SEPRA did not request or investigate anything, and the gendarmerie did not perceive sufficient interest from SEPRA to conduct its own investigation; - in terms of reliability: the statement was not spontaneous. The witness, who had heard the account of the BROYES (51) case prior to his interview, may naturally have been impressed by this account and drawn parallels with his own experience, thereby increasing its strangeness and unwittingly influencing certain aspects of his statement. Only a genuine on-site investigation would have allowed: - the exploration and perhaps validation of one of the physical hypotheses (see above) specific to this case; - or, conversely, confirm a sufficiently broad range of similarities between the two cases to consider them as stemming from the same phenomenon, and based on this, by cross-referencing the information: o potentially formulate hypotheses to explain this phenomenon; o at a minimum, increase the consistency of this observation to two testimonies. The strangeness of the two cases, although unequal, is significant. The consistency is too weak to support an unexplained nature in either case or in both. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the two cases as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Sighting of two balloons of unknown origin
description: On January 7, 2000, at approximately 7:20 PM, the pilot of a plane bound for Casablanca observed two balloons, one blue and one white, at a short distance below his aircraft. The balloons carried a payload resembling a radar reflector. Following a complaint, Météo-France (the French national meteorological service) indicated that they were not weather radiosondes. An investigation with the military yielded no new information. While the nature of the objects (balloons) seemed certain, their origin could not be determined.

summary: fleeting nighttime observation of a motionless shape reflected on an interior wall; instantaneous disappearance: lack of information.
description: Testimony of an observation made in the spring of 2000 (without a date of day, month, or time: arbitrary date of May 1, 2000) and collected in 2008. One evening in the spring of 2000, a 13-year-old boy observed a red light on the living room wall that seemed to come from outside. The witness then saw, for a few seconds, a motionless shape behind a window that disappeared instantly. Only one testimony was collected. This testimony was deemed unusable by GEIPAN (the French UFO investigation group). Indeed, the witness did not describe a UAP (Unidentified Aerial Phenomenon) but one or more lights on the ground or on a wall, without any possibility of linking it to a UAP because no UAP was described. The entire report was filed 8 or 9 years later, without a precise date. GEIPAN classifies this case as C: lack of information.
